newsitem.title: USA: State Farm Mutual seeks bank charter.
newsitem.headline: State Farm Mutual seeks bank charter.

text.p: State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co., the largest property and casualty insurance company in the nation, said Monday it was forming a subsidiary to enter the banking business in a sign of the increasingly blurred lines between sectors of the financial services industry.

"They have continued to blur and being able to be a full financial services provider is going to be a critical success factor in this evolving marketplace," said Larry Mayewski, an analyst at A.M. Best Co.
State Farm said it filed an application for a federal savings bank charter with the Office of Thrift Supervision and will soon file an application with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.
Earlier this month, Transamerica Corp., a $50 billion insurer based in San Francisco, made a similar application, and Mayewski said he would not be surprised if others followed suit.

State Farm's new financial institution, to be called State Farm Financial Services FSB, will offer a full range of financial products such as residential mortgage loans, home equity loans, automobile loans and leases, and credit cards.
The bank will also offer checking accounts, savings accounts, certificates of deposit and money market accounts.

State Farm said its new wholly owned banking subsidiary, which will have an initial capitalisation of $25 million, will not have branch offices. Instead, State Farm agents will help link customers to the bank.
State Farm officials said they expect the bank to open shortly after the applications are approved, which usually takes six months.

They added that State Farm Financial Services will begin operating in one or two states in its first year and expand conservatively in subsequent years. The company did not disclose the states where it will first operate.

A State Farm spokesman said the company had considered buying an existing bank before deciding to form its own banking business. "A lot of it was just that we wanted to build it to our own specifications," he said.

While insurance companies have been allowed to own a thrift for years, State Farm spokesman Steve Witmer said the changing competitive environment, in which banks will likely be allowed to offer more financial services -- including insurance -- prompted State Farm to seek to enter the banking business.
"There may be a day soon where consumers will expect to get banking and insurance from a single supplier," he said.
Technology considerations also made a banking unit more feasible at this point, Witmer said, adding that State Farm plans to offer some services via home computer.

David Taylor, executive vice president at the Bank Administration Institute, a research and education group for the banking industry, said forming a brand new bank makes sense for State Farm, which can sell banking products to its huge base of existing customers.
"From where they stand, it's really the right choice for them," Taylor said. "They're big and strong and they have the ability and the capability to leverage off their current customer base."
